html:
(1) An intrinsic motivational signal: empowerment as a dopaminergically encoded drive.

Empowerment cannot shape behavior unless the organism has some way to value increases in control: the system must convert "this state affords many reliably distinct futures" into an intrinsically appetitive signal that biases attention, exploration, and action selection. Classical motivation theories propose that organisms are not only driven by homeostatic deficits but also by an "effectance/competence" tendency to seek mastery and causal efficacy, and later work frames autonomy/competence as basic psychological needs–suggesting an evolution-installed preference for being an effective cause in the world, even when immediate extrinsic reward is absent 1, 2. Empirically, infants rapidly learn action→\rightarrowoutcome contingencies in paradigms like the mobile conjugate reinforcement task and show physiological/affective reactivity when contingency is violated (nonreinforcement), consistent with an early-emerging valuation of controllability (though this does not, by itself, resolve whether it is present "from birth" versus learned extremely quickly) 3, 4.

Importantly, even if the initial bias is weak or purely "curiosity-like," dopaminergic TD learning can rapidly bootstrap empowerment into a proxy for long-run reward: states and policies that expand controllable futures tend to (i) increase the chance of encountering extrinsic rewards, (ii) enable flexible switching when goals change, and (iii) reduce the expected cost of adverse events–so repeated experience causes value to back up onto high-empowerment regions of state space (see "Neuromodulators" for TD/RPE details and how evolution shaped dopaminergic circuits) 5, 6. Recent evidence that dopamine can carry value-free action-prediction errors (teaching which actions reliably produce which outcomes, not only which outcomes are rewarding) further supports a mechanistic bridge from "learn the channel" to "value the channel" 7, 8. The dual-controller model separates two candidate teaching signals (Figure).
